summary: Defines a CMS content type for compressed data. Compression before signing or encryption removes redundancy and reduces message size. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Squishing a message before locking it up makes it smaller and harder to crack. This is the standard envelope for a squished message.

questions: which compression algorithm does cms use
what is the compresseddata content type
subtitle: A standard envelope for compressing data before it is signed or encrypted in a CMS message.

tldr.problem: Compression helps before signing or encryption, but compression added at other levels (such as MIME or SSL) does not cover CMS content unless it is supplied by an external means.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3274 defines a CompressedData content type that carries a version of 0, a compression algorithm identifier and the content being compressed. ZLIB is the required algorithm.
tldr.outcome: CMS implementations SHOULD support the content type, and those that do MUST support ZLIB. Compressing before encryption can help security, but mixing secret and untrusted data can leak information.

today: RFC 3274 is a Proposed Standard, published in June 2002, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Compress Inside CMS
sections.content:
RFC 3274 describes a compressed-data content type for the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, defined in RFC 2630). It is implemented as a new ContentInfo type and extends the types CMS already defines. CMS implementations SHOULD include support for it.

The abstract lists the benefits of compressing before transmission: it removes data redundancy that could help an attacker, it speeds up later steps such as signing or encryption because there is less data, and it reduces overall message size. Proposals to add compression at the MIME or SSL level do not help CMS content unless the compression is supplied by an external means.
sections.eli5: Packing a suitcase tighter means a smaller bag to carry and lock. This RFC gives CMS a proper way to pack the suitcase first.

sections.title: The CompressedData Type
sections.content:
The content type is identified by the object identifier id-ct-compressedData, and its ASN.1 type is CompressedData, a SEQUENCE of three fields.

  • version: the syntax version number. It MUST be 0.
  • compressionAlgorithm: an identifier for the algorithm used.
  • encapContentInfo: the content that is compressed, which can be content of any type.

The format is written in ASN.1, and Appendix A gives the full ASN.1 module.
sections.eli5: The envelope has three boxes: a version number, the name of the squishing method, and the squished message itself.

sections.title: ZLIB Compression
sections.content:
CMS implementations that support CompressedData MUST support the ZLIB algorithm, defined in RFC 1950 and RFC 1951. The RFC points out that it has a freely available, portable and efficient reference implementation. It is identified by id-alg-zlibCompress and takes no parameters.

ZLIB offers compression levels from good but slow to less good but fast. The level is always compatible with the decompressor, so it does not need to be given as a parameter.

The parameters field SHOULD be omitted, but MAY be encoded as an ASN.1 NULL. The RFC explains that when the 1988 AlgorithmIdentifier syntax was translated into the 1997 syntax, the OPTIONAL on the parameters got lost and was later recovered, so some implementations encode NULL and some omit the field. Receivers may meet either encoding.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to understand one standard squishing method, ZLIB. There are fast squishes and thorough squishes, but any of them can be unsqueezed the same way.

sections.title: Advertising Support
sections.content:
Implementations SHOULD use the SMIMECapabilities attribute (see RFC 2633) to say they can process compressed content. A compression capability is just the AlgorithmIdentifier of the supported algorithm, which for this document is the ZLIB identifier.

That capability MUST be DER-encoded as the hexadecimal string 30 0D 06 0B 2A 86 48 86 F7 0D 01 09 10 03 08. Alternatively, compression may be handled by prior arrangement, for example as part of an interoperability profile.
sections.eli5: A program can tell others "I can unsqueeze ZLIB" with a fixed secret-code string, or people can simply agree beforehand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is not concerned with security, except that compressing before encryption can enhance the protection from other processing steps by reducing the quantity of known plaintext available to an attacker.

It also warns that combining security-sensitive material with possibly untrusted data before compression and encryption is risky. Information about the sensitive data may be inferred from knowing the untrusted data and the compression ratio.
sections.eli5: Squishing first hides some patterns, but if a sneaky person can add their own words next to your secret, how small it squishes can give hints about the secret.

sections.title: Identifiers and IANA
sections.content: The content type and algorithms are identified by object identifiers. They were assigned from an arc contributed to the S/MIME Working Group by RSA Security. If more compression algorithms appear, their advocates are expected to assign OIDs from their own arcs. No action by the IANA is necessary for this document or any anticipated updates.
sections.eli5: Each kind of envelope and squishing method has its own name tag. New methods make their own tags, so no central office needs to be asked.

items.title: compressionAlgorithm
items.text: Identifies the algorithm; ZLIB is required.
